extracted.intended_audience: PIs, grant writers, and research administrators preparing NIH R01 applications (especially applicants to NIDA/NIAAA and other ICs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points about whether to propose an NIH R01 as a modular (≤$250,000 direct costs) versus a traditional budget, and how budget size/format affects review and funding likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget amount relative to the modular limit ($250,000)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proposal requests direct costs at or below the $250,000 modular limit versus above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The $250,000 limit has never been adjusted and its spending power is about half what it was; the modular limit was designed to capture 90%+ of new R01s originally. Trend data and recent Notices of Grant Award suggest ICs are funding far fewer modular R01s — many successful R01s request >$250k. The post's data: only a small fraction of new R01s in NIAAA and NIDA are modular, implying modular requests are less likely to be awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope must match requested budget (the modular R01 doesn't pay for itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed scientific scope should be realistic given the budget requested; modular (smaller) budgets may not support the scope reviewers expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues modular budgets often cannot achieve the expected scope/production and therefore fare poorly in review. If the science requires spending power that $250k no longer provides, asking only for modular funds can lead to a weak application. Design scope to fit the real purchasing power of the budget requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers' expectations and career-review norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Review panels carry embedded expectations about necessary spending power; applicants should anticipate these norms when setting budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, career review criteria were formed when one grant provided sufficient spending power; applicants now up their budgets to match those expectations. Penalties for being 'too big' appear diminished, so reviewers may favor proposals that reflect historical spending power (i.e., larger budgets). Be mindful that review perceptions about appropriate budget size affect competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: IC-specific signals and Notices of Grant Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Different NIH Institutes and Centers may signal preferences about modular vs larger budgets; applicants should check IC guidance and award patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: NCI has been urging PIs to submit within the modular limit, while other ICs (e.g., NIDA, NIAAA) show very few modular awards. Look at an IC's funded R01s, Notices of Grant Award, and public guidance to infer whether modular submissions are being favored or disfavored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget formatting as a signal (round modular numbers vs non-round traditional budgets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the budget appears in round modular increments (divisible by $25,000) or as a traditional detailed/non-round request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round numbers divisible by $25,000 normally indicate a modular submission. Traditional budgets tend not to land on such round numbers. Applicants can signal intent by choosing modular formatting, but given funding patterns, modular-format requests may be less competitive in some ICs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic requesting for early-career investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of whether newbies should request the full modular limit or a somewhat lower modular amount to avoid perceptions of overreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older 'whisper wisdom' recommended early-career PIs ask for $225k or $200k rather than the $250k limit to avoid overreach. The author notes that this advice may be outdated given current trends favoring larger budgets; weigh IC norms and section culture before following it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire for and use of success-rate data comparing modular vs traditional submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate modular vs traditional strategy using empirical success-rate data broken down by budget size and IC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly states a desire to see NIH success rate data for modular versus non-modular proposals. Applicants and institutions should seek or request such data (by IC and fiscal year) to inform budgeting strategy rather than relying on anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inflation-adjusted (BRDPI) and nominal median cost trends when planning budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider historical inflation-adjusted and nominal median R01-equivalent costs to understand what a given dollar amount buys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites eLife figures showing median nominal dollars and BRDPI-adjusted medians over time: median total costs reached apparent asymptote (~$365k nominal) in 2010-2013 and rose after 2014. Use BRDPI-adjusted measures to compare spending power across years and set realistic budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position of your request within the distribution of requested direct costs (variability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where your requested budget sits relative to the distribution and variability of requested amounts for unsolicited RPGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 7A (eLife) shows changes in variability over time: many PIs clustered at the modular limit in earlier years, variability grew after 2014. Applicants should consider whether clustering at the modular limit or requesting a larger amount places them competitively within current variability patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lab-level strategy: number of grants versus budget per grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to aim for multiple smaller grants or fewer larger grants to achieve necessary lab spending power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes the historical shift from 'one grant lab' to 'two grant lab' and more recently PIs consolidating to one larger-budget grant. Choose a strategy (multiple grants vs one larger grant) based on realistic spending power needs and current funding climate.
